name: Under-eye filler (tear trough)

card.summary: Filler placed in the hollow under the eyes to soften shadowing; widely used and fairly well described, but a high-skill area where delayed swelling, lumps and rare vision-threatening events are documented.
card.note: Swelling after treatment is common; delayed lumps and rare orbital and vascular complications are reported in the literature.

quick.overview:
Tear trough filler is the injection of a soft gel, usually hyaluronic acid, into the groove between the lower eyelid and the cheek to reduce hollowing and dark shadows. It is used by clinicians as a non-surgical alternative to lower eyelid surgery.

On looksmaxxing forums it is mentioned as a small adjustment that can be noticeable in person without a plastic look. Medical literature describes it as common but technically demanding, with no standard evidence-based technique.
quick.mechanism: Filler placed in the tear trough camouflages the hollow and the bulge of orbital fat that creates a shadow, by adding volume under the skin [1]. HA was the most commonly reported product in delayed-complication cases, with poly-L-lactic acid and calcium hydroxylapatite also reported [2].
quick.risks: Swelling after infraorbital HA filler occurred in over half of patients in one retrospective review of 706 treatments, and was lower when a small amount of triamcinolone was mixed with the filler [4]. A systematic review of delayed complications identified swelling, lumps and xanthelasma-like reactions [2]. A first case of orbital compartment syndrome with retrobulbar haemorrhage after tear trough filler has been reported, managed without lasting visual loss [5].

lead: Under-eye filler, or tear trough filler, is the injection of a dermal filler, most often hyaluronic acid (HA), into the tear trough, the depression running from the inner corner of the eye toward the cheek, to soften hollowing and shadowing under the eyes [1][3]. Reviews state that dermal fillers can camouflage tear trough deformity and orbital fat pseudoherniation [1].

A systematic review of 42 articles on HA tear trough techniques found most evidence to be level III, with no standardized, evidence-based approach comparing needle and cannula injection [3]. A case series of 198 eyes in 100 patients, mostly female, evaluated HA filler as an alternative to lower eyelid surgery [8].

Documented complications include post-injection swelling, delayed lumps and discoloration, and rare orbital events [4][2][5]. Public interest in the procedure is visible in search data: Google Trends analysis found tear trough filler search interest changed by more than 50 percent within single weeks [6].

paras: The periorbital region can be treated with neuromodulators, which lift the brow and improve lines, and with fillers, which camouflage the tear trough and herniated orbital fat appearance [1]. A common technique described uses a blunt cannula along tailored linear paths, reported in a series of 1,452 tear trough applications between 2016 and 2020 [7]. Systematic review data found no significant difference in reported aesthetic results between needle and cannula approaches, and no standardised technique [3].

Evidence on effectiveness consists largely of retrospective, non-experimental studies; most of the 42 articles in one review were level III [3]. A consecutive case series of 198 eyes, followed on average 5.1 months, assessed patient satisfaction with an HA filler as an alternative to lower eyelid surgery [8]. Registered trials include a Phase 4 pilot of two HA fillers in the lower eyelid [10] and a study of an HA product versus no treatment for infra-orbital hollows [11].

A retrospective review of 447 patients and 706 infraorbital HA treatments reported swelling in 51 percent of patients not receiving triamcinolone, versus 23 percent when low-dose triamcinolone was mixed with the filler; swelling rose with the volume injected [4]. A systematic review of 52 cases of delayed complications found swelling the most common (42.3 percent), followed by lumps or nodules (25.0 percent) and xanthelasma-like reactions (17.3 percent); 98 percent were female, and HA was the most reported product [2]. A case report described orbital compartment syndrome from retrobulbar haemorrhage after tear trough filler, treated with surgery with no lasting visual compromise, described as the first such report [5]. Wikipedia describes blindness after fillers as rare but typically permanent [13].

Human research includes systematic reviews of techniques and delayed complications [3][2], retrospective cohorts [4][7], a consecutive case series [8], and a case report of an orbital complication [5]. Registered trials include a platelet-rich fibrin study for tear trough rejuvenation [9], a two-filler pilot [10] and a study of RHA Redensity Eye versus no treatment [11]. No randomized trial identified here examines under-eye filler for young men seeking an appearance goal.

A looksmax.org user reported having tear trough and jaw filler in one session, described little downtime apart from swelling and said the total cost was $450; replies were mostly mocking or asked for photos [12]. Treatment is described in communities as a small correction that can be noticeable in person without looking plastic.

lore.intro: Under-eye filler appears in forums mainly as personal reports of a minor adjustment rather than a core 'hardmaxx' procedure [12].

claims.claim: Tear trough filler gives a noticeable improvement without a plastic look and with little downtime.
claims.believers: A poster reports a noticeable difference in person with only some swelling and no other downtime [12].
claims.experts: Retrospective data show swelling in over half of patients after infraorbital HA filler [4], and a case series reported patient satisfaction over about five months of follow-up [8].

claims.claim: Tear trough filler is low risk.
claims.experts: Reviews list delayed swelling, nodules and discoloration [2] and a case report documents orbital compartment syndrome [5].
